Monday: Thomas looked at the plan for a model water lift: pulleys, buckets, a motor, a painted base. Too much for two weeks. He wrote: "Version one: one pulley, one bucket, a hand crank. It only has to lift water." Deepak wanted the motor first. "If we finish nothing, the motor doesn't matter," Thomas said.

Wednesday: The crank version lifted a cup of water, slowly and with a wobble. They showed it to the teacher, who said the string kept slipping and the bucket was too heavy.

Saturday: With that feedback they fixed the string, swapped the bucket, and only then added the second pulley. The motor stayed a plan for next time.

qa.q: What did the first version of the water lift have?
qa.a: It had one pulley, one bucket and a hand crank.

qa.q: What does Thomas think about aiming for a perfect model, and how does he feel about it?
qa.a: Thomas thinks a perfect model might never be finished, and feels sensible and determined to get something working first.

qa.q: What could the group do if the teacher's feedback asks for a big change, and why?
qa.a: They could pick the one fix that matters most and do that first, because small steady improvements keep a working version alive.

qa.q: How might Deepak see leaving the motor for later?
qa.a: Deepak may feel disappointed at first, having wanted the motor, but seeing a working crank version likely makes waiting easier.

grounding: The group first builds a simple working version, shows it to the teacher for feedback, and then improves features, instead of aiming for a perfect model that may not be finished in time.

Yamini, sit. You're trying to make the perfect robot for your competition, yes? Let me tell you what your Devika maasi learned at fifteen.

Our school had a science fair, and my group wanted to build a model of an automatic railway crossing: gates, lights, a bell, a train on tracks. Everything. My friend drew twenty pages of plans.

Our physics teacher looked at them and said, "Show me something that works by Friday. Just the gate going up and down."

We were insulted. But we did it: one cardboard gate, one motor, one switch. On Friday it worked. The teacher said, "Now the train should trigger it." So we added a sensor. Then the light. The bell we never finished.

But the gate moved on fair day, and the group that planned everything showed only drawings.

qa.q: What did the teacher ask to see by Friday?
qa.a: Just the gate going up and down.

qa.q: How did the group feel when the teacher asked for only a simple version?
qa.a: They felt insulted and a bit deflated, since they had twenty pages of plans for something far bigger.

qa.q: Which choice in the story mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Agreeing to build the simple gate first mattered most; it gave them a working base they could improve with feedback, so something moved on fair day.

qa.q: How might the group that planned everything have felt on fair day?
qa.a: They likely felt disappointed and perhaps envious, having only drawings to show next to a working gate.

grounding: An elder recalls a group building a simple working version first, getting a teacher's feedback and then adding features instead of aiming for a perfect model.

The electricity had gone out across their part of Srinagar again, and the district science exhibition was eight days away. Imran and Rehana sat by a window in Imran's house with a torch, staring at their plan: a greenhouse model with automatic watering, a temperature display and a fan.

"We won't finish all this," Rehana said. "Not with power cuts every evening." She pushed her hair back.

Imran rubbed his forehead. "Then let's make the smallest thing that works. A box, a plant, a pipe that drips when we press a button."

They built it in two days, on battery. On Monday they showed it to their teacher, who said, "Good. Now make the drip start when the soil is dry."

That took three more days. The fan and display never got built.

At the exhibition, their drip worked every time. A judge asked what they would add next. Rehana had an answer ready.

qa.q: How many days away was the exhibition at the start?
qa.a: The exhibition was eight days away.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling when she said they would not finish everything?
qa.a: Rehana felt worried and realistic, anxious that power cuts would leave them with a half-built model.

qa.q: What else could the pair do to protect the model from the power cuts?
qa.a: They could keep a spare set of batteries and test the drip on battery each day, since the whole model must run without mains power.

qa.q: How might the teacher see the pair's approach?
qa.a: The teacher likely felt pleased and encouraged, because a small working model gave something concrete to give feedback on.

grounding: Shows a pair, under power cuts and time pressure, building a simple working version first, getting teacher feedback and then improving it.
